blocks.text: 1. DiskANN

blocks.alt: A collection larger than memory uses DiskANN to build a disk-based graph

blocks.text: DiskANN covers how vector search can scale beyond what fits in memory, closing out the ANN Search Algorithms module by tying every earlier idea into one final constraint.
It closes the module by covering search over data stored on disk rather than held entirely in memory.
2. Every Algorithm So Far Assumed Memory
Every algorithm covered so far assumed the entire index fits comfortably in memory.
Some collections grow far too large for that assumption to hold at all.
3. When A Collection Outgrows Memory

blocks.alt: An in-memory index is compared against a disk-based index

blocks.text: Compression alone, as seen with IVF-PQ, can only shrink an index so far.
A truly massive collection still eventually exceeds available memory even when compressed.
4. A Graph Stored On Disk

blocks.alt: A graph is stored on disk

blocks.text: DiskANN stores a navigable graph similar to HNSW, but primarily on disk.
Search traverses that graph the same way, just reading nodes from disk instead of memory.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Algorithm","Where the graph lives"],"rows":[["HNSW","Primarily in memory"],["DiskANN","Primarily on disk, with a memory cache"]]}

blocks.text: 5. Minimizing Disk Reads

blocks.alt: A query minimizes disk reads to produce results

blocks.text: Disk reads are dramatically slower than memory access, by orders of magnitude.
DiskANN is engineered specifically to minimize the number of disk reads a search actually needs.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: A single disk read can take orders of magnitude longer than a memory access, meaning DiskANN's entire design centers on touching disk as few times as possible per query.

blocks.text: 6. Caching Frequently Accessed Nodes

blocks.alt: A frequently accessed node gets cached in memory

blocks.text: A small, carefully chosen portion of the graph stays cached in memory.
Those cached nodes cover the most commonly visited parts of a typical search path.
7. Compressed Vectors In DiskANN

blocks.alt: A full vector compresses into a compressed vector stored on disk

blocks.text: Much like the compression used within IVF-PQ clusters, DiskANN often keeps compressed vector representations in memory for a fast initial pass.
Full precision data gets read from disk only when a candidate needs verification.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: Keeping compressed vectors in memory while full precision data waits on disk mirrors the same layered approach already seen in IVF-PQ and ScaNN, applied here specifically to bridge memory and disk rather than speed and accuracy.

blocks.text: 8. Cost Versus Scale Tradeoff
Disk storage is far cheaper per gigabyte than memory.
DiskANN trades some query latency for dramatically lower infrastructure cost at massive scale.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Storage strategy","Cost and latency profile"],"rows":[["Fully in memory, like HNSW","Lower latency, higher infrastructure cost"],["DiskANN","Somewhat higher latency, dramatically lower cost at scale"]]}

blocks.text: 9. Recognizing When DiskANN Is The Right Choice

blocks.alt: A dataset exceeding available RAM points toward using DiskANN

blocks.text: Collections too large or too costly to fit entirely in memory need DiskANN.
Collections that comfortably fit in memory benefit more from HNSW or IVF's lower latency.
10. Worked Example
The example below demonstrates simulating disk versus cached memory access costs during a graph traversal.

code.content:
import random
import time

cached_nodes = set(range(0, 50))

def simulate_node_access(node_id, cached_nodes):
    if node_id in cached_nodes:
        return "memory", 0.0001
    else:
        return "disk", 0.01  # simulated disk read is far slower

def simulate_graph_traversal(path, cached_nodes):
    total_time = 0
    disk_reads = 0
    memory_reads = 0
    for node_id in path:
        source, cost = simulate_node_access(node_id, cached_nodes)
        total_time += cost
        if source == "disk":
            disk_reads += 1
        else:
            memory_reads += 1
    return total_time, disk_reads, memory_reads

search_path = [random.randint(0, 500) for _ in range(20)]
total_time, disk_reads, memory_reads = simulate_graph_traversal(search_path, cached_nodes)

print(f"Search path length: {len(search_path)} nodes")
print(f"Memory reads: {memory_reads}")
print(f"Disk reads: {disk_reads}")
print(f"Simulated total access time: {total_time:.4f} seconds")

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: Running this example shows the total simulated time dominated by disk reads even though they are far fewer in count than memory reads.

blocks.text: 11. Common Mistakes

items: Assuming DiskANN performs as fast as a fully in memory algorithm like HNSW.
Underestimating the importance of caching frequently accessed nodes in memory.
Choosing DiskANN for a collection that would comfortably fit in memory anyway.
Ignoring the cost versus latency tradeoff when deciding between DiskANN and memory based algorithms.

blocks.text: 12. ANN Search Algorithms: Module Complete

items: Brute Force Search introduced the exact, simplest baseline that every faster method is measured against.
KNN generalized single nearest neighbor search into finding the K closest vectors.
ANN introduced the general tradeoff of accepting a small accuracy risk for much faster search.
HNSW covered navigating a layered graph of connected vectors for logarithmic time search.
IVF covered clustering vectors and searching only the most relevant clusters.
IVF-PQ covered combining clustering with vector compression for even greater efficiency.
Product Quantization covered the compression technique behind IVF-PQ in full depth.
LSH covered a hashing based alternative that groups similar vectors into shared buckets.
ScaNN covered combining partitioning, scoring, and rescoring into one layered pipeline.
DiskANN closed the module by covering search that scales beyond what fits in memory.
Next up: Retrieval, covering how search results actually get turned into usable context for a RAG system.
